title: Rain, Quakes, and Red Tape: Peshawar's Race to Save the Homes Where Bollywood Began
excerpt: The ancestral houses of Dilip Kumar and Raj Kapoor have survived a century in Peshawar's old city. They may not survive another monsoon season.
body:
The Kapoor Haveli in Peshawar's Qissa Khwani Bazaar was once a place where stories were born — literally. It was here that Prithviraj Kapoor, patriarch of Indian cinema's most storied dynasty, grew up before migrating to Bombay in the 1920s. His son Raj Kapoor, the 'Showman of Indian Cinema,' would carry Peshawar's soul into every frame of his work. A few lanes away, in Mohallah Khudadad, another future legend — Muhammad Yusuf Khan, later Dilip Kumar — took his first breaths in 1922.

A century later, both houses are falling apart.

## Crumbling Under Neglect

Heritage experts and local activists issued fresh warnings this week that the two structures could collapse at any time. The April 3 earthquake that rattled Khyber Pakhtunkhwa weakened Kapoor Haveli's already compromised walls, while continuous pre-monsoon rains have accelerated the damage. At Dilip Kumar's house, roofs of several rooms have caved in entirely. Walls are crumbling into debris with each rainfall.

"The government, instead of preserving these historical landmarks, has abandoned them," said Shakil Waheedullah, secretary of the Cultural Heritage Council, KPK. Residents who live and work beside the buildings describe deep structural cracks and a pervasive sense of inevitability.

Both houses were declared national heritage by Pakistan's government in 2016. In 2021-22, the Khyber Pakhtunkhwa government approved PKR 2.35 crore to purchase both properties and convert them into museums. In July 2025, a further PKR 33.8 million was allocated for restoration and conservation. None of that money has produced visible results.

## A Pattern of Promises

The disconnect between announcements and action is by now a familiar rhythm. The World Bank's KITE (Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Integrated Tourism Development) project earmarked PKR 200 million for the restoration, envisioning heritage museums that would celebrate the actors' contributions to cinema and boost Peshawar's tourism economy. The Directorate of Archaeology drew up plans. Provincial officials spoke of preserving cultural heritage.

Yet five years after the initial purchase decision, neither property has a functional roof, let alone a museum exhibit.

A provincial government official, speaking on condition of anonymity, acknowledged the gap: "The government cannot carry out the preservation work due to a lack of funds and other resources." The official insisted, however, that the government remains "serious" about the museum conversions.

For the Director of Archaeology and Museums, Abdul Samad, the partial collapse of Dilip Kumar's house was, paradoxically, a "blessing in disguise" — it provides an opportunity to reconstruct the structure entirely under the KP Antiquities Act 2016, since engineers had deemed the original building irreparable.

## Why It Matters to the Diaspora

For millions of Indians — and particularly those in the diaspora — Dilip Kumar and Raj Kapoor are not just film stars. They are cultural touchstones, bridges between the subcontinent's shared past and its partitioned present. Their Peshawar homes carry a significance that transcends cinema: they are physical reminders that India and Pakistan's cultural heritage is intertwined in ways that no border can fully sever.

NRIs who trace their own roots to undivided India's northwest — from Peshawar to Lahore to Rawalpindi — feel this loss acutely. Every collapsed wall is a piece of shared memory gone. For second-generation diaspora members, these homes represent a tangible connection to family narratives that otherwise exist only in grandparents' stories.

The pre-monsoon season is weeks away. Without immediate intervention, the next round of heavy rains could finish what neglect and earthquakes have started. Heritage activists in Peshawar are clear: the time for official statements has passed. What remains is a race against weather, gravity, and institutional inertia — one that Bollywood's golden age deserves not to lose.
